raw_response.overlap_rationale: Both full texts are accessible and authored or led by Nandita Singh, drawing on multi-site ethnographic fieldwork on rural drinking water supply and community water treatment in India. Study A (Singh 2006) analyzes 2002-2004 fieldwork in 12 villages across two districts of Madhya Pradesh (Datia and Shivpuri) and 15 villages across three districts of West Bengal, focusing on adult women's participation in Panchayati Raj Institution water committees (WCWHCs) and NGO-initiated arsenic removal plant committees, including case studies of public handpumps sited in dominant-caste localities in MP and purity/pollution barriers in WB. Study B (Singh et al. 2008) examines children's (especially girl children's) realization of the human right to water using broader multi-site Indian fieldwork (dates unspecified) that includes 18 villages with 55 handpumps in Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, and Jharkhand, 44 public handpumps in Madhya Pradesh and Bihar (only 9 sited in backward-caste localities), fluoride removal plants in MP, arsenic removal plants in West Bengal, and rural/urban pockets. Thus, the two papers are neither duplicates nor exact same-sample companion reports, as Study B includes additional states (Bihar, Jharkhand, and a note on Gujarat), fluoride plants, and handpump-level counts focused on children, whereas Study A focuses on governance committees in 12 MP and 15 WB villages. However, both draw on Singh's overlapping rural fieldwork on public handpump caste-locality siting in Madhya Pradesh and community arsenic removal plants in West Bengal, creating partial sample overlap and moderate double-counting risk if caste-based exclusion from rural handpumps or arsenic plants is synthesized across both studies without adjustment. Confidence is medium because Study B omits exact fieldwork dates and district/village names, preventing exact quantification of the village-level intersection in MP and WB.
raw_response.study_a_sample_and_data: Ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2002 and 2004 across 27 rural villages in India: 12 villages in two districts of Madhya Pradesh (Datia and Shivpuri, including villages Lamkana and Saprar) and 15 villages in three districts of West Bengal (including village Raipara). Data collection comprised participant observation (including Panchayat/committee meetings), structured and unstructured key-informant interviews, an earlier opinion survey in 12 village Panchayats, and 12 focus group discussions (5 exclusively with women), with roughly two-thirds of participants involved in local water governance bodies (PRI Women and Child Welfare and Health Committees in MP and NGO-initiated arsenic removal plant water quality management committees in WB).
raw_response.study_b_sample_and_data: Interdisciplinary actor-oriented and sociology-of-law analysis drawing on multi-site field observations in India (collection dates not stated), reporting empirical subsets including: (1) 18 villages with 55 handpumps installed under rural water supply programmes in Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, and Jharkhand (24 rejected by mothers for drinking/cooking); (2) 44 public handpumps in villages of Madhya Pradesh and Bihar (only 9 located in backward-section localities); and (3) qualitative field observations of arsenic removal plants and treated surface-water taps in West Bengal, fluoride removal plants in Madhya Pradesh, and unspecified rural and urban pockets, examining barriers to children's and girl children's right to safe water.
